description: Domain knowledge, system design, OS, DBMS, CN, OOP, algorithms, and company-specific technical interview questions with pseudocode, implementations, and explanations for placement preparation.

questions.question: What are the four pillars of Object-Oriented Programming?
questions.answer: The four pillars of OOP are: (1) Encapsulation – bundling data and methods within a class and restricting direct access using access modifiers. (2) Abstraction – hiding implementation details and exposing only necessary features. (3) Inheritance – a child class inherits properties and methods from a parent class, enabling code reuse. (4) Polymorphism – the ability of a function or object to take on multiple forms through overloading (compile-time) and overriding (runtime).
questions.pseudocode:
// Encapsulation
CLASS BankAccount:
    PRIVATE balance = 0
    PUBLIC FUNCTION deposit(amount):
        balance += amount
    PUBLIC FUNCTION getBalance():
        RETURN balance

// Inheritance
CLASS Animal:
    FUNCTION speak(): PRINT 'Some sound'

CLASS Dog EXTENDS Animal:
    FUNCTION speak(): PRINT 'Woof'   // Overriding (Polymorphism)

// Abstraction
ABSTRACT CLASS Shape:
    ABSTRACT FUNCTION area()

CLASS Circle EXTENDS Shape:
    FUNCTION area(): RETURN PI * r * r

example.encapsulation: Private balance + public deposit/withdraw in BankAccount class
example.abstraction: Abstract Vehicle class with move() method implemented differently by Car and Bike
example.polymorphism: Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak(); // calls Dog's speak at runtime

questions.question: What is the difference between abstract class and interface in Java?

abstract_class.definition: A class that cannot be instantiated and may contain both abstract and concrete methods.
abstract_class.when_to_use: When classes share a common base and some default behavior.
features: Methods can have any access modifier

interface.definition: A pure contract. All methods are abstract by default (Java 7). Java 8+ allows default and static methods.
interface.when_to_use: To define a contract for unrelated classes and achieve multiple inheritance.
features: A class can implement multiple interfaces

questions.pseudocode:
// Abstract Class
ABSTRACT CLASS Vehicle:
    STRING brand
    FUNCTION start():    // concrete method
        PRINT 'Starting engine'
    ABSTRACT FUNCTION fuelType()  // must be implemented

CLASS Car EXTENDS Vehicle:
    FUNCTION fuelType(): RETURN 'Petrol'

// Interface
INTERFACE Flyable:
    FUNCTION fly()   // abstract by default

INTERFACE Swimmable:
    FUNCTION swim()

CLASS Duck EXTENDS Animal IMPLEMENTS Flyable, Swimmable:
    FUNCTION fly(): PRINT 'Duck flying'
    FUNCTION swim(): PRINT 'Duck swimming'

questions.question: Explain method overloading vs method overriding.

overloading.definition: Same method name, different parameters. Resolved at compile time (static polymorphism).
overloading.example: int add(int a, int b) vs double add(double a, double b)

overriding.definition: Subclass redefines a parent method with the same signature. Resolved at runtime (dynamic polymorphism).

answer.key_difference: Overloading = compile-time polymorphism. Overriding = runtime polymorphism.

questions.pseudocode:
// Overloading (same class, different params)
CLASS Calculator:
    FUNCTION add(a, b): RETURN a + b
    FUNCTION add(a, b, c): RETURN a + b + c   // overloaded
    FUNCTION add(a: FLOAT, b: FLOAT): RETURN a + b   // overloaded

// Overriding (parent → child, same signature)
CLASS Animal:
    FUNCTION speak(): PRINT 'Generic animal sound'

CLASS Cat EXTENDS Animal:
    FUNCTION speak(): PRINT 'Meow'   // overrides parent

animal = NEW Cat()
animal.speak()   // prints 'Meow' — runtime decision

questions.question: What is a constructor? What are the types of constructors?
questions.answer: A constructor is a special method invoked automatically when an object is created. It has the same name as the class and no return type. Types: (1) Default constructor – no parameters, provided by compiler if none defined. (2) Parameterized constructor – takes arguments to initialize object with specific values. (3) Copy constructor – creates a new object as a copy of an existing object.
questions.pseudocode:
CLASS Student:
    STRING name
    INT age

    // Default Constructor
    FUNCTION Student():
        name = 'Unknown'
        age = 0

    // Parameterized Constructor
    FUNCTION Student(n, a):
        name = n
        age = a

    // Copy Constructor
    FUNCTION Student(other: Student):
        name = other.name
        age = other.age

// Usage
s1 = NEW Student()             // default
s2 = NEW Student('Alice', 20) // parameterized
s3 = NEW Student(s2)          // copy

questions.question: What is the difference between IS-A and HAS-A relationships?
questions.answer: IS-A represents inheritance: a Dog IS-A Animal. HAS-A represents composition: a Car HAS-A Engine. IS-A uses 'extends' (Java) or class inheritance. HAS-A uses object composition — an object contains another object as a field. Composition is generally preferred over inheritance for flexibility.
questions.pseudocode:
// IS-A (Inheritance)
CLASS Animal:
    FUNCTION breathe()

CLASS Dog EXTENDS Animal:   // Dog IS-A Animal
    FUNCTION bark()

// HAS-A (Composition)
CLASS Engine:
    FUNCTION start()

CLASS Car:
    engine = NEW Engine()   // Car HAS-A Engine
    FUNCTION drive():
        engine.start()
        PRINT 'Car moving'

questions.question: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy?
questions.answer: Shallow copy creates a new object but copies references to the original's nested objects. Deep copy creates a completely independent copy including all nested objects. Shallow copy is faster but both objects share inner state. Deep copy is safe but more expensive.

questions.question: What is the difference between a stack and a queue?
questions.pseudocode:
// STACK (using array)
STACK:
    data = []
    FUNCTION push(x): data.append(x)
    FUNCTION pop():
        IF data is EMPTY: ERROR 'Stack underflow'
        RETURN data.removeLast()
    FUNCTION peek(): RETURN data[last]
    FUNCTION isEmpty(): RETURN data.size == 0

// QUEUE (using array)
QUEUE:
    data = []
    FUNCTION enqueue(x): data.append(x)
    FUNCTION dequeue():
        IF data is EMPTY: ERROR 'Queue underflow'
        RETURN data.removeFirst()
    FUNCTION front(): RETURN data[0]
    FUNCTION isEmpty(): RETURN data.size == 0

questions.question: What is a Binary Search Tree (BST) and what are its properties?
questions.answer: A BST is a binary tree where for each node: all values in the left subtree are less than the node, and all values in the right subtree are greater. Search, insert, delete are O(log n) average, O(n) worst case for a skewed tree. Balanced variants like AVL and Red-Black trees guarantee O(log n) in all cases.
questions.pseudocode:
// BST Insert
FUNCTION insert(root, value):
    IF root is NULL:
        RETURN NEW Node(value)
    IF value < root.data:
        root.left = insert(root.left, value)
    ELSE IF value > root.data:
        root.right = insert(root.right, value)
    RETURN root

// BST Search
FUNCTION search(root, target):
    IF root is NULL: RETURN FALSE
    IF root.data == target: RETURN TRUE
    IF target < root.data: RETURN search(root.left, target)
    RETURN search(root.right, target)

// BST Inorder Traversal (gives sorted output)
FUNCTION inorder(root):
    IF root is NULL: RETURN
    inorder(root.left)
    PRINT root.data
    inorder(root.right)

questions.question: Explain Big O notation with common complexities.

answer.definition: Big O describes the upper bound (worst case) of an algorithm's time or space growth as input size n increases.

common_complexities.O(1): Constant – array index access, hash map lookup

questions.pseudocode:
// O(1) – Constant
FUNCTION getFirst(arr): RETURN arr[0]

// O(n) – Linear
FUNCTION findMax(arr):
    max = arr[0]
    FOR each x in arr:
        IF x > max: max = x
    RETURN max

// O(n^2) – Quadratic
FUNCTION bubbleSort(arr):
    FOR i FROM 0 TO n-1:
        FOR j FROM 0 TO n-i-2:
            IF arr[j] > arr[j+1]:
                SWAP arr[j], arr[j+1]

// O(log n) – Binary Search
FUNCTION binarySearch(arr, target):
    left = 0, right = n-1
    WHILE left <= right:
        mid = (left + right) / 2
        IF arr[mid] == target: RETURN mid
        IF arr[mid] < target: left = mid + 1
        ELSE: right = mid - 1
    RETURN -1

questions.question: What is a Hash Map / Hash Table? How does it work?
questions.answer: A hash map stores key-value pairs. A hash function maps a key to a bucket index. Ideal time complexity for get/put is O(1). Collisions (two keys mapping to same index) are handled via chaining (linked list at bucket) or open addressing (probing for next empty slot).
questions.pseudocode:
// Hash Map Structure
HASHMAP:
    buckets = ARRAY of size N (each bucket is a list)

    FUNCTION hashFunction(key):
        RETURN key.hashCode() % N

    FUNCTION put(key, value):
        index = hashFunction(key)
        FOR each (k, v) in buckets[index]:
            IF k == key: UPDATE v; RETURN
        buckets[index].append((key, value))

    FUNCTION get(key):
        index = hashFunction(key)
        FOR each (k, v) in buckets[index]:
            IF k == key: RETURN v
        RETURN NULL

// Chaining to handle collision:
// bucket[3] → [(key1, val1) → (key2, val2)] // both hash to 3

questions.question: What is a Heap? Explain Min-Heap and Max-Heap.
questions.answer: A heap is a complete binary tree satisfying the heap property. In a Min-Heap, every parent is smaller than its children (root = minimum). In a Max-Heap, every parent is greater (root = maximum). Heaps are implemented as arrays and used in priority queues and heap sort. Insert and delete are O(log n), peek is O(1).
questions.pseudocode:
// Min-Heap Insertion (heapify up)
FUNCTION insert(heap, value):
    heap.append(value)
    i = heap.size - 1
    WHILE i > 0:
        parent = (i - 1) / 2
        IF heap[parent] > heap[i]:
            SWAP heap[parent], heap[i]
            i = parent
        ELSE: BREAK

// Extract Min (heapify down)
FUNCTION extractMin(heap):
    min = heap[0]
    heap[0] = heap[last]
    heap.removeLast()
    i = 0
    WHILE TRUE:
        left = 2*i + 1, right = 2*i + 2
        smallest = i
        IF left < size AND heap[left] < heap[smallest]: smallest = left
        IF right < size AND heap[right] < heap[smallest]: smallest = right
        IF smallest == i: BREAK
        SWAP heap[i], heap[smallest]
        i = smallest
    RETURN min

questions.question: What is a Graph? Explain DFS and BFS traversals.
questions.answer: A graph is a collection of nodes (vertices) connected by edges. DFS (Depth-First Search) explores as deep as possible before backtracking — uses a stack/recursion. BFS (Breadth-First Search) explores all neighbors at the current level before going deeper — uses a queue.
questions.pseudocode:
// DFS (Recursive)
FUNCTION dfs(graph, node, visited):
    IF node in visited: RETURN
    visited.add(node)
    PRINT node
    FOR each neighbor in graph[node]:
        dfs(graph, neighbor, visited)

// BFS (Iterative)
FUNCTION bfs(graph, start):
    visited = SET()
    queue = QUEUE()
    queue.enqueue(start)
    visited.add(start)
    WHILE queue is NOT EMPTY:
        node = queue.dequeue()
        PRINT node
        FOR each neighbor in graph[node]:
            IF neighbor NOT in visited:
                visited.add(neighbor)
                queue.enqueue(neighbor)

// Use DFS for: cycle detection, path finding, topological sort
// Use BFS for: shortest path (unweighted), level-order traversal

questions.question: What is Dynamic Programming? Explain with the Fibonacci example.
questions.answer: Dynamic Programming (DP) solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing results to avoid recomputation. Two approaches: Memoization (top-down, recursive with cache) and Tabulation (bottom-up, iterative). DP applies when a problem has optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems.

questions.question: Explain Merge Sort and Quick Sort with pseudocode. Compare their complexities.

merge_sort.strategy: Divide and Conquer – split array in half, recursively sort, merge

quick_sort.strategy: Divide and Conquer – pick pivot, partition array around it, recursively sort
quick_sort.time: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst (bad pivot)

questions.pseudocode:
// MERGE SORT
FUNCTION mergeSort(arr):
    IF arr.length <= 1: RETURN arr
    mid = arr.length / 2
    left = mergeSort(arr[0..mid])
    right = mergeSort(arr[mid+1..])
    RETURN merge(left, right)

FUNCTION merge(left, right):
    result = []
    i = 0, j = 0
    WHILE i < left.length AND j < right.length:
        IF left[i] <= right[j]: result.append(left[i]); i++
        ELSE: result.append(right[j]); j++
    APPEND remaining elements
    RETURN result

// QUICK SORT
FUNCTION quickSort(arr, low, high):
    IF low < high:
        pivotIndex = partition(arr, low, high)
        quickSort(arr, low, pivotIndex - 1)
        quickSort(arr, pivotIndex + 1, high)

FUNCTION partition(arr, low, high):
    pivot = arr[high]
    i = low - 1
    FOR j FROM low TO high-1:
        IF arr[j] <= pivot:
            i++
            SWAP arr[i], arr[j]
    SWAP arr[i+1], arr[high]
    RETURN i + 1

questions.question: What are ACID properties in databases?

answer.atomicity: All-or-nothing: if any part of a transaction fails, the entire transaction is rolled back.
answer.consistency: A transaction brings the database from one valid state to another, maintaining all constraints.
answer.isolation: Concurrent transactions execute independently — intermediate states are invisible to others.
answer.durability: Once committed, a transaction persists even through system failures.

questions.question: Explain all types of SQL JOINs with examples.

answer.inner_join: Returns rows with matches in BOTH tables.
answer.left_join: All rows from left + matching from right; unmatched right = NULL.
answer.right_join: All rows from right + matching from left; unmatched left = NULL.
answer.full_outer_join: All rows from both; unmatched sides = NULL.
answer.cross_join: Cartesian product — every combination of rows from both tables.
answer.self_join: A table joined with itself to compare rows within the same table.

questions.pseudocode:
// INNER JOIN – only matched rows
SELECT E.name, D.dept_name
FROM Employee E
INNER JOIN Department D ON E.dept_id = D.id

// LEFT JOIN – all employees, dept may be NULL
SELECT E.name, D.dept_name
FROM Employee E
LEFT JOIN Department D ON E.dept_id = D.id

// SELF JOIN – find employees with same manager
SELECT A.name AS Employee, B.name AS Manager
FROM Employee A
JOIN Employee B ON A.manager_id = B.id

// FULL OUTER JOIN – all rows from both
SELECT E.name, D.dept_name
FROM Employee E
FULL OUTER JOIN Department D ON E.dept_id = D.id

questions.question: What is normalization? Explain 1NF, 2NF, 3NF with examples.

answer.definition: Normalization organizes a database to reduce redundancy and improve integrity.
answer.1NF: Atomic values only. No repeating groups. Each row must be unique.
answer.2NF: 1NF + no partial dependency: non-key attributes must depend on the WHOLE primary key.
answer.3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependency: non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes.
answer.BCNF: Stricter 3NF: every determinant must be a candidate key.

questions.question: What is the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases?

sql.use_when: Structured data, complex relationships, ACID compliance required

nosql.structure: Flexible schema: document, key-value, wide-column, graph
nosql.use_when: Unstructured/semi-structured data, massive scale, flexible schema

questions.question: What are indexes in a database and why are they used?
questions.answer: An index is a data structure (usually a B-tree or hash) that allows the database to find rows quickly without scanning the entire table. It speeds up SELECT queries but slows down INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations slightly because the index must be maintained. Indexes should be created on columns used frequently in WHERE, JOIN, or ORDER BY clauses.

questions.question: What is a stored procedure and how is it different from a function?
questions.answer: A stored procedure is a precompiled set of SQL statements stored in the database. It can perform actions (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and may or may not return a value. A function must return a value and cannot perform actions like INSERT/DELETE directly. Stored procedures are called with EXEC/CALL; functions are used in SELECT statements.

questions.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?

process.definition: A program in execution with its own memory space, registers, and resources.
process.isolation: Fully isolated — one crash doesn't affect others.
process.communication: Via IPC: pipes, sockets, shared memory

thread.definition: A lightweight unit of execution within a process, sharing the process's memory.
thread.isolation: Not isolated — a buggy thread can crash the whole process.
thread.communication: Via shared memory — needs synchronization (mutex, semaphore)

questions.pseudocode:
// Process Creation (fork in Unix)
PROCESS main:
    child = fork()     // creates a new process
    IF child == 0:
        // child process code
        PRINT 'I am the child'
    ELSE:
        // parent process code
        PRINT 'I am the parent'

// Thread Creation
FUNCTION task():
    PRINT 'Thread running'

thread1 = NEW Thread(task)
thread2 = NEW Thread(task)
thread1.start()
thread2.start()
thread1.join()   // wait for thread1 to finish
thread2.join()
// Both threads share the same process memory

questions.question: What is deadlock? Explain with an example and the four necessary conditions.

answer.definition: Deadlock is a situation where two or more processes are permanently waiting for resources held by each other — none can proceed.

conditions.mutual_exclusion: Resources cannot be shared — only one process holds a resource at a time.
conditions.hold_and_wait: A process holds a resource while waiting to acquire another.
conditions.no_preemption: Resources cannot be forcibly taken away.
conditions.circular_wait: A circular chain: P1 waits for P2's resource, P2 waits for P1's resource.

questions.question: What is virtual memory? How does paging work?

answer.virtual_memory: Gives each process the illusion of a large contiguous memory even when physical RAM is limited, using disk (swap space) as an extension.

paging.definition: Virtual memory is divided into fixed-size pages, physical memory into frames of the same size.
paging.page_table: Maps virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers.
paging.page_fault: When a required page is not in RAM, the OS loads it from disk — called a page fault.

questions.question: What are CPU scheduling algorithms? Explain with examples.
questions.answer: CPU scheduling decides which process runs next on the CPU. Common algorithms: FCFS (First-Come First-Served), SJF (Shortest Job First), Round Robin, Priority Scheduling, and Multilevel Queue.

questions.question: What is the difference between mutex and semaphore?

mutex.definition: A mutual exclusion lock. Only the thread that locked it can unlock it. Binary (locked/unlocked).
mutex.use_case: Protecting a critical section — only one thread at a time.

semaphore.definition: A signaling mechanism with a counter. Can be binary (0/1) or counting (0..N).
semaphore.use_case: Controlling access to a pool of resources or producer-consumer synchronization.

questions.pseudocode:
// MUTEX – Critical Section
mutex = NEW Mutex()

FUNCTION incrementCounter():
    mutex.lock()         // only one thread enters
    counter = counter + 1
    mutex.unlock()       // release for others

// SEMAPHORE – Counting
semaphore = NEW Semaphore(3)  // max 3 concurrent users

FUNCTION accessDatabase():
    semaphore.wait()     // decrement count; block if 0
    // use database connection
    semaphore.signal()   // increment count; wake a blocked thread

// Producer-Consumer with Semaphore
empty = Semaphore(N)   // N empty slots
full = Semaphore(0)    // 0 filled slots

PRODUCER:
    empty.wait()         // wait for empty slot
    ADD item to buffer
    full.signal()        // signal item available

CONSUMER:
    full.wait()          // wait for item
    REMOVE item from buffer
    empty.signal()       // signal slot freed

questions.question: What is the OSI model? Explain all 7 layers.

layers.name: Application
layers.function: User-facing protocols: HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS

layers.name: Presentation
layers.function: Data formatting, encryption, compression: SSL/TLS, JPEG

layers.name: Session
layers.function: Session management between apps: NetBIOS, RPC

layers.name: Transport
layers.function: End-to-end delivery, error recovery: TCP, UDP

layers.name: Network
layers.function: Routing and logical addressing: IP, ICMP, routers

layers.name: Data Link
layers.function: Frame transmission, MAC addressing: Ethernet, switches

layers.name: Physical
layers.function: Raw bit transmission: cables, hubs, NIC

answer.mnemonic: All People Seem To Need Data Processing (7 → 1)

questions.pseudocode:
// Data flow through OSI layers (sending side)
APPLICATION: HTTP request created
    ↓ add HTTP header
PRESENTATION: data encrypted (TLS)
    ↓ add encryption info
SESSION: session token added
    ↓ add session header
TRANSPORT: data split into segments, port numbers added (TCP)
    ↓ add TCP header
NETWORK: segments wrapped in packets, IP addresses added
    ↓ add IP header
DATA LINK: packets wrapped in frames, MAC addresses added
    ↓ add frame header+trailer
PHYSICAL: frames converted to bits and sent over wire

// Receiving side: reverse (remove headers layer by layer)

questions.question: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?
What happens when you type www.google.com in a browser?
answer: 1. Browser checks its DNS cache for the IP of google.com
2. If not found, OS checks /etc/hosts, then queries DNS resolver
3. DNS resolver recursively queries Root → TLD (.com) → Authoritative nameserver → returns IP
4. Browser initiates TCP 3-way handshake with the IP
5. TLS handshake establishes encrypted HTTPS channel
8. Browser parses HTML, fetches CSS/JS/images, renders the page
questions.pseudocode:
// Step-by-step browser flow
FUNCTION loadPage(url):
    // DNS Resolution
    ip = checkBrowserCache(url)
    IF ip is NULL:
        ip = checkOSCache(url)
    IF ip is NULL:
        ip = dnsResolve(url)   // queries DNS servers

    // TCP Connection
    socket = TCP.connect(ip, port=443)
    TLS.handshake(socket)     // for HTTPS

    // HTTP Request
    request = 'GET / HTTP/1.1\nHost: www.google.com\n...'
    socket.send(request)

    // HTTP Response
    response = socket.receive()
    html = response.body

    // Rendering
    dom = parseHTML(html)
    cssom = parseCSS(fetchCSS())
    renderTree = combine(dom, cssom)
    paint(renderTree)         // display on screen

questions.question: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS? What is SSL/TLS?
questions.answer: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) transfers data in plain text — readable by anyone on the network. HTTPS adds a security layer using SSL/TLS, encrypting the data between client and server. TLS (Transport Layer Security) uses asymmetric encryption for handshake (key exchange) and symmetric encryption for data transfer.

questions.question: What is subnetting and what is a subnet mask?
questions.answer: Subnetting divides a large network into smaller sub-networks for efficiency and security. A subnet mask distinguishes the network portion from the host portion of an IP address. CIDR notation like /24 means 24 bits are the network part, leaving 8 bits for hosts (256 addresses).

questions.question: How would you design a URL shortener like bit.ly?

components.api_gateway: Routes requests to shortening or redirect service
components.shortening_service: Generates 6-char base62 key from auto-incremented ID
components.cache: Redis: cache hot short URLs to reduce DB lookups
components.redirect_service: Looks up key in cache/DB, returns 301/302 redirect

questions.question: How would you design a Parking Lot System?

functional: Support multiple floors and spot sizes

questions.pseudocode:
// Object-Oriented Design
CLASS ParkingSpot:
    id: STRING
    floor: INT
    size: ENUM [SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE]
    isOccupied: BOOLEAN
    FUNCTION canFitVehicle(vehicle): RETURN vehicle.size <= self.size

CLASS Vehicle:
    licensePlate: STRING
    size: ENUM [MOTORCYCLE, CAR, TRUCK]

CLASS Ticket:
    ticketId: STRING
    vehicle: Vehicle
    spot: ParkingSpot
    entryTime: DATETIME
    exitTime: DATETIME
    amount: FLOAT

CLASS ParkingLot:
    floors: LIST of Floor
    activeTickets: MAP<licensePlate, Ticket>

    FUNCTION parkVehicle(vehicle):
        spot = findAvailableSpot(vehicle.size)
        IF spot is NULL: RETURN 'Lot Full'
        spot.isOccupied = TRUE
        ticket = NEW Ticket(vehicle, spot, now())
        activeTickets[vehicle.licensePlate] = ticket
        RETURN ticket

    FUNCTION exitVehicle(licensePlate):
        ticket = activeTickets[licensePlate]
        ticket.exitTime = now()
        duration = ticket.exitTime - ticket.entryTime
        ticket.amount = calculateFee(duration, ticket.spot.size)
        ticket.spot.isOccupied = FALSE
        REMOVE from activeTickets
        RETURN ticket

    FUNCTION calculateFee(duration, spotSize):
        rate = { SMALL: 10, MEDIUM: 20, LARGE: 30 }  // per hour
        hours = ceil(duration / 3600)
        RETURN hours * rate[spotSize]

questions.question: How would you design a Rate Limiter?
questions.answer: A rate limiter restricts the number of requests a client can make in a time window to prevent abuse and ensure fair usage.

algorithms.token_bucket: Tokens added at fixed rate. Each request consumes a token. Allows bursts.
algorithms.leaky_bucket: Requests processed at a fixed rate. Excess requests are queued or dropped.
algorithms.fixed_window: Count requests in a fixed time window (e.g., 100 req/min).
algorithms.sliding_window: Uses a rolling time window — more accurate than fixed window.

questions.pseudocode:
// Token Bucket Algorithm
CLASS TokenBucket:
    capacity: INT         // max tokens
    tokens: FLOAT         // current tokens
    refillRate: FLOAT     // tokens per second
    lastRefill: TIMESTAMP

    FUNCTION allowRequest():
        now = currentTime()
        elapsed = now - lastRefill
        tokens = MIN(capacity, tokens + elapsed * refillRate)
        lastRefill = now

        IF tokens >= 1:
            tokens -= 1
            RETURN TRUE   // request allowed
        RETURN FALSE      // rate limit exceeded

// Redis-based Sliding Window (distributed)
FUNCTION isAllowed(userId, limit, windowSeconds):
    key = 'ratelimit:' + userId
    now = currentTimestampMs()
    windowStart = now - windowSeconds * 1000

    REDIS: ZREMRANGEBYSCORE(key, 0, windowStart)  // remove old requests
    count = REDIS: ZCARD(key)                     // count current requests

    IF count < limit:
        REDIS: ZADD(key, now, now)                // add current request
        REDIS: EXPIRE(key, windowSeconds)
        RETURN TRUE
    RETURN FALSE

What is Docker? What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?
questions.answer: Docker is a containerization platform that packages applications with their dependencies into portable units called containers. A Docker image is a read-only template (like a class). A container is a running instance of an image (like an object). Images are stored in registries (Docker Hub, ECR). Containers are isolated but share the host OS kernel — lighter than VMs.
questions.pseudocode:
// Dockerfile – blueprint for an image
FROM python:3.11
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ['python', 'app.py']

// Build image from Dockerfile
docker build -t myapp:v1 .

// Run a container from the image
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 myapp:v1

// List running containers
docker ps

// Stop and remove container
docker stop <container_id>
docker rm <container_id>

// Docker Compose – multi-container apps
services:
  web:
    image: myapp:v1
    ports: ['8000:8000']
  db:

questions.question: What is CI/CD? Explain the pipeline.
questions.answer: CI (Continuous Integration) automatically builds and tests code when changes are pushed. CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment) automatically delivers tested code to staging or production. Together they reduce manual errors and release cycles.
questions.pseudocode:
// Typical CI/CD Pipeline

// 1. DEVELOPER pushes code to GitHub
git commit -m 'Add feature X'
git push origin main

// 2. CI Pipeline triggers automatically (e.g., GitHub Actions)
PIPELINE:
    STAGE 'Build':
        RUN 'npm install' OR 'pip install -r requirements.txt'
        RUN 'npm run build'

    STAGE 'Test':
        RUN 'npm test'        // unit tests
        RUN 'pytest'          // integration tests
        IF tests fail → STOP, notify developer

    STAGE 'Code Quality':
        RUN 'eslint src/'     // linting
        RUN 'sonarqube scan'  // static analysis

    STAGE 'Docker Build':
        RUN 'docker build -t myapp:latest .'
        RUN 'docker push registry/myapp:latest'

    STAGE 'Deploy to Staging':
        RUN 'kubectl apply -f k8s/staging/'
        RUN smoke tests

    STAGE 'Deploy to Production' (CD):
        IF manual_approval: DEPLOY
        RUN 'kubectl apply -f k8s/prod/'
        MONITOR metrics → rollback if error rate spikes

questions.question: What is recursion? Explain with the Tower of Hanoi problem.
questions.answer: Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive function must have a base case (stopping condition) and a recursive case. The Tower of Hanoi moves n disks from source to destination using an auxiliary peg.
questions.pseudocode:
// RECURSION Template
FUNCTION solve(problem):
    IF base_case: RETURN result        // stop condition
    smaller = reduce(problem)
    RETURN combine(solve(smaller))     // recursive call

// TOWER OF HANOI
FUNCTION hanoi(n, source, destination, auxiliary):
    IF n == 1:
        PRINT 'Move disk 1 from ' + source + ' to ' + destination
        RETURN
    hanoi(n-1, source, auxiliary, destination)   // move n-1 to aux
    PRINT 'Move disk ' + n + ' from ' + source + ' to ' + destination
    hanoi(n-1, auxiliary, destination, source)   // move n-1 to dest

// Call: hanoi(3, 'A', 'C', 'B')
// Time: O(2^n), Space: O(n) call stack

// FACTORIAL (simpler recursion)
FUNCTION factorial(n):
    IF n == 0 OR n == 1: RETURN 1       // base case
    RETURN n * factorial(n - 1)         // recursive case

questions.question: What is the difference between pass by value and pass by reference?
questions.answer: Pass by value: a copy of the variable is passed. Changes inside the function do not affect the original. Pass by reference: the memory address of the variable is passed. Changes inside the function affect the original. In Java, primitives are passed by value; objects are passed by reference (the reference is copied, but the object is shared).
questions.pseudocode:
// PASS BY VALUE (primitives)
FUNCTION increment(x):   // x is a copy
    x = x + 1
    PRINT x    // prints 11

a = 10
increment(a)
PRINT a        // still 10 — original unchanged

// PASS BY REFERENCE (objects)
FUNCTION addItem(list, item):  // list is a reference
    list.append(item)

myList = [1, 2, 3]
addItem(myList, 4)
PRINT myList   // [1, 2, 3, 4] — original changed!

// POINTER (C/C++)
FUNCTION swapByRef(a: *INT, b: *INT):
    temp = *a
    *a = *b
    *b = temp

x = 5, y = 10
swapByRef(&x, &y)
PRINT x, y   // 10, 5

questions.question: What are design patterns? Explain Singleton and Factory patterns.
questions.answer: Design patterns are reusable solutions to commonly occurring software design problems. The Singleton pattern ensures only one instance of a class exists. The Factory pattern provides a way to create objects without specifying the exact class.
questions.pseudocode:
// SINGLETON PATTERN
CLASS DatabaseConnection:
    STATIC instance = NULL

    PRIVATE CONSTRUCTOR DatabaseConnection():
        // connect to DB

    STATIC FUNCTION getInstance():
        IF instance is NULL:
            instance = NEW DatabaseConnection()
        RETURN instance

// Usage:
conn1 = DatabaseConnection.getInstance()
conn2 = DatabaseConnection.getInstance()
// conn1 and conn2 are the SAME object

// FACTORY PATTERN
INTERFACE Shape:
    FUNCTION draw()

CLASS Circle IMPLEMENTS Shape:
    FUNCTION draw(): PRINT 'Drawing Circle'

CLASS Rectangle IMPLEMENTS Shape:
    FUNCTION draw(): PRINT 'Drawing Rectangle'

CLASS ShapeFactory:
    STATIC FUNCTION createShape(type: STRING): Shape
        IF type == 'circle': RETURN NEW Circle()
        IF type == 'rectangle': RETURN NEW Rectangle()
        RAISE 'Unknown shape type'

// Usage:
shape = ShapeFactory.createShape('circle')
shape.draw()   // 'Drawing Circle'
// Caller doesn't need to know which class to instantiate
